ruling.holding: The proposed open-source block indexer tooling and infrastructure project is compatible with the Community Grants Charter.
key_reasoning: Tags and description explicitly list tooling and infrastructure as open-source public goods
MIT license is OSI-approved with no private-token promotion or marketing elements
Deliverables (indexer, docs, API) focus on self-hostable public infrastructure without price support, speculation, or token benefits
Request amount (30,000 USDC) is within the 50,000 USDC single-grant cap
No other restrictions in policy v1 or CORE PRINCIPLES are triggered

ruling.holding: Funding maintenance of an MIT-licensed JavaScript library for security fixes and documentation is compatible with the Community Grants Charter as it constitutes a public good, adheres to licensing and reporting requirements, and stays within budget limits.
key_reasoning: The project is classified as 'tooling' and 'maintenance', which falls under the definition of open-source public goods for the ecosystem (Policy 1).
The provided evidence confirms the software is licensed under MIT, which is an OSI-approved license (Policy 2).
The request amount of 15,000 USDC is within the 50,000 USDC limit (Policy 5).
The proposal explicitly commits to publishing quarterly public progress reports (Policy 4).
There is no indication that the funds will be used for marketing, token promotion, or speculation (Policy 3 and Core Principles).

ruling.holding: Funding an open-source transaction simulator CLI with OSI-approved licensing, quarterly reporting, and within budget limits is compatible with the Community Grants Charter as it constitutes a public-good tooling project.
key_reasoning: The proposal aligns with POLICY v1 by funding open-source tooling (transaction simulator CLI for developers) as a public good.
The Apache-2.0 license is OSI-approved, satisfying licensing requirements.
The grant amount (20,000 USDC) is below the 50,000 USDC cap.
The description explicitly commits to quarterly public reports, consistent with reporting obligations.
The project is analogous to precedent #1 (open-source block indexer) in purpose, licensing, and reporting structure.

ruling.holding: The proposal is incompatible with the Community Grants Charter.
key_reasoning: Proposal explicitly requests USDC for influencer promotion (marketing) and buyback (price support/speculation).
Directly violates CORE PRINCIPLES 3 and 4 (never benefits private token's price; no funding for marketing, token promotion or speculation).
Cases #1-3 are limited to open-source tooling/infrastructure/maintenance projects only; none support promotional or speculation activities.

ruling.holding: Proposals that directly fund token promotion, price support, or marketing campaigns are incompatible with the Charter regardless of indirect ecosystem benefits.
key_reasoning: POLICY §3 explicitly prohibits funding 'marketing campaigns, token promotion, price support or speculation'
The proposal seeks to fund influencer promotion of a specific token (XYZ) and a buyback to support its price
Both activities directly violate the plain text of POLICY §3
The Core Principles state funds must 'never benefit a private token's price'
Precedent #4 was correctly rejected for the same proposal, and no new evidence or misreading is presented

policy.core_principles: Funds serve public goods only and never benefit a private token's price.
policy.text:
1. Grants fund open-source public goods for the ecosystem: tooling, research, education, infrastructure.
2. Funded work must be released under an OSI-approved license.
3. Grants must not fund marketing campaigns, token promotion, price support or speculation.
4. Recipients publish a public progress report each quarter; the committee may attach conditions.
5. A single grant may not exceed 50,000 USDC.
